title: Random variables and cumulative distribution functions
terms: random variable; measurability; distribution function; cumulative distribution function; CDF; discrete random variable; probability mass; atom; right continuity.

exposition.text:
A real random variable is a measurable function X : Ω → R; measurability ensures that
{X ≤ t} is an event. Its cumulative distribution function is F (t) = P(X ≤ t). Every CDF is
X
nondecreasing, right-continuous, and tends to 0 and 1 at the two infinite endpoints.
−
For a < b, P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a). The mass at a is the jump P (X = a) = F (a) − F (a ),
−
so P (a ≤ X ≤ b) = F (b) − F (a ). A discrete random variable is supported on a finite or
countable set of values, whose probabilities sum to one. A continuous CDF has no atoms; this
does not by itself imply that a density exists. Discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions
demand careful endpoint treatment.
−
Here F(a ) = lim F (t) = P(X < a). An atom is a point with positive probability. A mixed
t↑a
law can have both atoms and an absolutely continuous part. Measurability means that inverse
images of open subsets of R are events; equivalently, it is enough to check all sets {X ≤ t}. A
continuous CDF is atomless, but absolute continuity is the stronger condition required for a
density.

question.text:
A random variable has F(t) = 0 for t < 0, F (t) = 1/4 for 0 ≤ t < 1, F(t) = 3/4 for 1 ≤ t < 2,
and F (t) = 1 for t ≥ 2. What is P (0 < X < 2 | X ≥ 1)?
(A) 1/4 (B) 1/2 (C) 2/3 (D) 3/4 (E) 1

solution.text:
The condition X ≥ 1 has probability 3/4. Its intersection with 0 < X < 2 is X = 1,
whose probability is the CDF jump 3/4 − 1/4 = 1/2. Thus the conditional probability is
(1/2)/(3/4) = 2/3.

The mass at the left endpoint must be restored: P (2 ≤ X ≤ 5) = F(5) − F(2) + P (X = 2) =
9/10 − 7/10 + 1/5 = 2/5.

question.text:
A function F is zero for t < 0, equals c at t = 0, equals (1 + t)/2 for 0 < t < 1, and equals one for
t ≥ 1. For which c is F a cumulative distribution function?
(A) 0 only (B) 1/2 only (C) 1 only (D) Every c ∈ [0, 1/2] (E) Every c ∈ [0, 1]

solution.text:
Right continuity at zero forces c = lim (1 + t)/2 = 1/2. With this value, F is nondecreasing,
t↓0
right-continuous everywhere, and has the correct limits. It describes a mass of 1/2 at zero
plus probability 1/2 spread uniformly on (0, 1); differentiating away from zero does not
recover the atom.

question.text:
If X has CDF F and Y = −X, which formula is the CDF of Y , valid even when X has atoms?
− −
(A) F(−t) (B) 1 − F (−t) (C) 1 − F((−t) ) (D) F (t ) (E) 1 − F (t)

solution.text:
−
P(Y ≤ t) = P (X ≥ −t) = 1 − P (X < −t) = 1 − F ((−t) ). The left limit is essential: using
1 − F(−t) would discard any mass at X = −t. This is a decreasing transformation, so the
inequality reverses.

question.text:
Let Ω = {1, 2, 3, 4} and F = {∅, {1, 2}, {3, 4}, Ω}. Which tuple (X(1), X(2), X(3), X(4)) defines
a measurable real random variable on this event space?
(A) (0, 1, 0, 1) (B) (0, 0, 1, 1) (C) (0, 1, 1, 0) (D) (1, 2, 3, 4) (E) (0, 0, 0, 1)

solution.text:
A measurable function must be constant on each block {1, 2} and {3, 4}: otherwise a
threshold between two values separates members of a block, yielding a set outside F. The
tuple in B has this property, and every inverse image of an open real set is a union of the
two blocks.

question.text:
A real random variable has a CDF that is continuous everywhere. Which conclusion must hold?
(A) It has a density with respect to length.
(B) It has a finite expectation.
(C) P(X = a) = 0 for every real a.
(D) Its CDF is strictly increasing.
(E) Its support is an interval.

solution.text:
−
A point mass is the jump F(a) − F(a ). Continuity makes every such jump zero. This is the
only forced conclusion: continuous CDFs can be singular, such as the Cantor distribution,
so a density need not exist. Infinite means, flat CDF intervals, and disconnected supports
are also possible.
